openingProblem.problem: In 1991 Yeltsin stood on a tank to defend democracy. In 1993 he sent tanks against his own parliament, and in 1999 he handed power to a former KGB officer. Did Yeltsin build Russian democracy, or undermine it?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: was Yeltsin a builder or an underminer of democracy?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Shock therapy and privatisation, 1992–1994
chunks.body:
When the Soviet Union ended, Boris Yeltsin had to build a new state, a market economy and a new political system at the same time. He chose speed. In January 1992 Prime Minister Yegor Gaidar's **shock therapy** programme freed most prices, and Anatoly Chubais began the privatisation of state enterprises.

The economist Stefan Hedlund explains the theory. Enterprises were told that their direct financial links to the state budget would be cut. Once managers knew that subsidies would not come, they would have to produce goods that could be sold at prices covering their costs. The whole transition was expected to take about half a year, after which the economy would grow without foreign support.

By the summer of 1992, Hedlund writes, "it became painfully evident that the project was failing". Enterprises did not look for markets; they stopped paying. Lost subsidies were met by unpaid taxes and wages; unpaid bills from customers by refusals to pay suppliers. Because there was no bankruptcy law, enterprises cut output but did not close. Inflation ended 1992 at well over 2,000 per cent. This mattered because savings and wages lost their value within months, which meant that most Russians experienced the market first as impoverishment.

**Privatisation** followed. Small shops and services were sold from January 1992. In June the mass privatisation programme was adopted, and in October every citizen received vouchers worth 10,000 rubles, then about 50 dollars, to exchange for shares. Most enterprises chose the option that gave 51 per cent of shares to their employees at a discount. By the end of June 1994, 70 per cent of enterprises had been privatised. Marie Lavigne notes that the government put the political aim, creating a class of owners as quickly as possible, ahead of efficiency.

The speed had a price. Notorious deals showed insiders acquiring large assets with very little cash, and the former Soviet *nomenklatura* took advantage of a process that lacked transparency and clear legal rules. Richard Sakwa concludes that the lack of accountability over privatisation "allowed massive insider dealing". Judt goes further, calling it "privatization as kleptocracy". Shock therapy and privatisation changed who owned Russia; they did not create the institutions, courts, laws and regulation that make a market work.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Shock therapy freed prices fast but produced hyperinflation and a chain of non-payment, not a working market.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Some market analysts argued the problem was too little shock, not too much (Hedlund).

argumentsThatWork.claim: Voucher privatisation transferred ownership quickly, which was its political aim.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Ownership changed but restructuring and corporate governance did not follow.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Without laws and accountability, privatisation enriched insiders.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Some insider ownership was the price of speed: employees received 51 per cent in the most popular option.

howItGetsAsked: To what extent did shock therapy fail to transform the Russian economy between 1992 and 1998?
Compare and contrast the economic crises of 1992 and 1998 in Russia.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Shock therapy failed in 1992 because enterprises responded to the loss of subsidies by not paying, rather than by selling.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Hedlund shows that unpaid subsidies were met by unpaid taxes and wages, and that inflation ended 1992 at well over 2,000 per cent.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that prices were free but the market did not work, because enterprises without a bankruptcy law could survive without customers.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, some market analysts argued that the reforms failed because there was too little shock, not too much.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Shock therapy therefore freed prices but failed to create a market, because the institutions a market needs were missing.

chunks.title: President against parliament: the crisis of 1993
chunks.body:
Russia began independence with the constitution of 1978, a Brezhnev-era document that gave authority to the Supreme Soviet. The parliament had granted Yeltsin emergency powers for the first year of reform. As shock therapy bit, a deep divide opened between the executive and the legislature, led by Speaker Ruslan Khasbulatov and Yeltsin's own Vice-President, Alexander Rutskoi. Yeltsin replaced Gaidar with an industrialist, Viktor Chernomyrdin, as a compromise, but on 12 March 1993 the Congress stripped him of his emergency powers. He narrowly survived an impeachment vote and called a referendum for 25 April, which showed, Peter Reddaway notes, that a small majority still trusted him.

The conflict ended in violence. On 21 September 1993 Yeltsin issued **decree 1400**, annulling the powers of the legislature and calling elections for a new parliament and a referendum on a new constitution, both on 12 December. The Supreme Soviet at once voted to impeach him and installed Rutskoi as acting president; on 23 September the congress confirmed the impeachment by 636 votes to 2. Deputies barricaded themselves in the parliament building, the White House, and the government cut off its electricity.

On 3 October a march by supporters of parliament broke through the cordon, and Rutskoi urged the crowd to storm the city hall, the Kremlin and the Ostankino television centre. The next day tanks bombarded the White House and the remaining deputies surrendered. According to the Kremlin, 143 people were killed; the human rights group Memorial estimated several hundred.

For the next three months, Reddaway writes, Yeltsin "exercised virtually dictatorial powers". He shut down the Constitutional Court, abolished regional and city legislatures and banned some nationalist and communist parties and publications. On 12 December voters approved a new constitution creating a strong presidential republic, with a two-chamber Federal Assembly and a president limited to two four-year terms. The vote was weaker than it looked: turnout was 54.8 per cent, and only about 31 per cent of all eligible voters supported the constitution. Yeltsin called the vote a "plebiscite", avoiding the 1990 law that required a majority of all registered voters for constitutional change. The same day, voters punished the reformers: Zhirinovsky's nationalist Liberal Democratic Party and the Communists beat Gaidar's liberals.

This mattered because Russia's new constitution was born from force, which meant that the presidency it created was strong but its legitimacy was contested from the start. Reddaway's verdict is that Yeltsin's resort to violence instead of compromise "seriously undermined Russia's infant democracy".

argumentsThatWork.claim: The root of the 1993 crisis was the clash over shock therapy between a reforming president and a parliament elected under Soviet rules.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Reddaway argues Yeltsin chose confrontation and made only minimal concessions, so the crisis was also a choice.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin won by force and wrote a super-presidential constitution.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Parliament's leaders also used violence on 3 October, and Rutskoi's side was no more democratic.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1993 settlement was legally weak from the start.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The constitution came to be generally regarded as legitimate and lasted.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the constitutional crisis of 1993 in Russia.
Discuss the view that Yeltsin did more to undermine democracy in Russia than to build it.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The violent end of the 1993 crisis left Russia with a strong presidency but a contested democracy.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Tanks bombarded the White House on 4 October, the Kremlin admitted 143 dead, and for three months Yeltsin shut the Constitutional Court and abolished regional legislatures.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the constitution approved on 12 December was imposed by the winner of a armed conflict, so its legitimacy rested on force as much as consent.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the parliament's leaders had also used violence, and Rutskoi had urged the crowd to storm the Kremlin and Ostankino.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The crisis therefore strengthened the state but weakened democracy, as Reddaway argues.

chunks.title: Chechnya, the oligarchs and the 1996 election
chunks.body:
Yeltsin tried to hold the federation together by bargaining. A series of bilateral treaties gave republics, especially Tatarstan, more autonomy than the constitution laid down. One republic refused to bargain. **Chechnya** had declared independence in 1991 and would not recognise Moscow's authority. Hardliners in Yeltsin's administration organised an invasion on 11 December 1994, expecting a quick victory. Instead the war lasted until August 1996. Johanna Nichols estimates that it killed between 2 and 10 per cent of Chechnya's population, mostly civilians. Sakwa calls the decision to intervene "perhaps his greatest mistake".

The war was one of four problems Yeltsin faced before the presidential election of June 1996. The Communists had dominated the Duma elections of 1995; his health was failing, and he had collapsed in October 1995; and his approval ratings were in single digits. Some advisers urged him to cancel the election.

He did not. He sacked his most liberal ministers, including Foreign Minister Andrei Kozyrev, and floated a new peace plan for Chechnya. Anatoly Chubais, dismissed in January after privatisation scandals, returned to run the campaign with Yeltsin's daughter Tatiana Dyachenko. Yeltsin toured the country handing out political favours. The campaign was bankrolled by the **oligarchs**, a small group of businessmen who had made vast fortunes in privatisation and wanted to protect them; the Kremlin even admitted exceeding the legal spending cap. Yeltsin failed to win a majority in the first round and faced the Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov in a run-off. Between the rounds he suffered a heart attack, which was hidden from voters until he had won.

The oligarchs had already gained from the state. In privatisation's second phase, Ann Robertson writes, a handful of businessmen "snatched up key enterprises at deep discount". After 1996 the price of their support was paid. Sakwa's judgement is that the alliance with the oligarchs won Yeltsin a second term "but at the price of allowing a form of oligarchic capitalism to flourish". This mattered because the state that won the 1996 election was dependent on private fortunes, which meant that after 1996 power and property were bound together in a way the voters could not control. Yeltsin, operated on in November 1996, was effectively an invalid for months, and much of the business of government passed to his closest advisers, known as "the Family".

argumentsThatWork.claim: Chechnya was Yeltsin's greatest failure: a war expected to be quick lasted until 1996 and cost many civilian lives.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Chechnya's refusal to recognise Moscow was a real threat to the federation, as other republics negotiated.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin won in 1996 by allying with the oligarchs, which tied the state to private wealth.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: He also won because many voters feared a Communist return under Zyuganov.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Bargaining with the regions held Russia together but weakened the centre.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Treaties with Tatarstan avoided another Chechnya.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the impact of the war in Chechnya on Yeltsin's presidency between 1994 and 1996.
Analyse the reasons why Yeltsin won the presidential election of 1996.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Yeltsin won the 1996 election mainly because the oligarchs financed a campaign he could not otherwise have fought.
useItInAnEssay.prove: With approval ratings in single digits, he relied on a campaign run by Chubais and bankrolled by the oligarchs, and the Kremlin admitted exceeding the spending cap.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a deeply unpopular president could outspend his rivals and reach a run-off against Zyuganov.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the oligarchs backed Yeltsin to protect what they had gained, so the decisive factor was also the fear of a Communist return.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The oligarchs' money was therefore the necessary condition of his victory, and its price was oligarchic capitalism.

chunks.title: 1998, the succession and Yeltsin's record
chunks.body:
Yeltsin's second term was marked by a declining economy, rising corruption and what Robertson calls "prime minister roulette". After a slight recovery in 1997, Paul Gregory writes, stubborn budget deficits and a poor business climate left Russia exposed when a global financial crisis began. In March 1998 Yeltsin dismissed Chernomyrdin. Sergei Kiriyenko lasted until August. That month the **rouble collapsed** and the government defaulted on its debts. Many banks became insolvent, living standards fell sharply, and GDP dropped 5 per cent in 1998. Yeltsin then tried Chernomyrdin again, then Yevgeny Primakov (September 1998 to May 1999), then Sergei Stepashin, and on 16 August 1999 Vladimir Putin, a former KGB officer whom he had made head of the Federal Security Service in 1998 and now named as his successor. A second war in Chechnya began late in 1999.

On New Year's Eve 1999 Yeltsin announced his resignation on television. Under the constitution Prime Minister Putin became acting president; his first act was to grant Yeltsin immunity from prosecution. On 26 March 2000 Putin was elected president in the first round. Robertson notes that Yeltsin needed a successor who could protect him and his family, whose complicity in corruption schemes was a growing concern.

How should Yeltsin's record be judged? The economic verdict is severe. Hedlund calculates that between 1991 and 1998 Russia lost around 40 per cent of its GDP and more than 80 per cent of capital investment, and Judt calls it the biggest peacetime setback for a major economy in modern history. Average inflation from 1992 to 2000 was 38 per cent. Growth returned only in 1999 and 2000, at 5.4 and 8.3 per cent, mainly because of the weak rouble and rising oil prices. Hedlund reports that the majority view now blames shock therapy itself, not just its execution.

The political verdict is more mixed. Sakwa argues that Yeltsin's claim to be the "father of Russian democracy" is "not without substance": he accepted the post-Soviet borders, held elections and left office voluntarily. But democracy at the close of his presidency "was far from consolidated". The 1993 constitution had been imposed by force, the 1996 election won with oligarchs' money, and power handed to a chosen successor. This mattered because the institutions Yeltsin left were strong at the top and weak everywhere else, which meant that his successor inherited a powerful presidency with few checks on it.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The 1998 crash showed that the market economy built in the 1990s was fragile.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Recovery came quickly in 1999–2000, so the crash also cleared the way for growth.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin's choice of successor was shaped by the need to protect himself and his family.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Putin's succession followed the constitution: the prime minister became acting president.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Yeltsin's record is economic failure combined with an unconsolidated but real democracy.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Elections were held and he left office voluntarily, unlike his Soviet predecessors.

howItGetsAsked: Discuss the view that Yeltsin did more to undermine democracy in Russia than to build it.
Compare and contrast the economic crises of 1992 and 1998 in Russia.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The financial crisis of August 1998 exposed how fragile Russia's new market economy was.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The rouble collapsed, the government defaulted on its debts, many banks became insolvent and GDP fell 5 per cent in 1998.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the stabilisation achieved since 1992 rested on borrowing and a budget the state could not balance, so one external shock brought it down.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, GDP grew 5.4 per cent in 1999 and 8.3 per cent in 2000, helped by the weak rouble and rising oil prices.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The crash was therefore a verdict on the 1990s, but not the end of Russian recovery.

historiography.argument: Shock therapy failed: by summer 1992 the project was failing, and between 1991 and 1998 Russia lost around 40 per cent of GDP; the majority view now holds that the policy itself, not too little of it, was at fault.
historiography.useItLikeThis: Hedlund's view supports the claim that the economic collapse of the 1990s came from the choice of shock therapy, which suggests Yeltsin's economic failure was a matter of policy, not only of circumstance.

historiography.argument: Yeltsin's claim to be the 'father of Russian democracy' is 'not without substance', but democracy at the close of his presidency was 'far from consolidated'; Chechnya was perhaps his greatest mistake.
historiography.useItLikeThis: Sakwa's argument allows a balanced judgement: it supports the claim that Yeltsin kept the democratic path open while showing why the institutions he left were weak.

misconceptions.wrong: Shock therapy quickly created a working market economy.
misconceptions.right: By summer 1992 it was **failing**: hyperinflation, non-payment, and no bankruptcy law (Hedlund).

misconceptions.wrong: The 1993 constitution was approved by a majority of Russians.
misconceptions.right: Only **about 31 per cent** of eligible voters supported it; turnout was 54.8 per cent.

misconceptions.wrong: The war in Chechnya was a quick success.
misconceptions.right: It began on 11 December 1994, was expected to be quick, and **lasted until August 1996**.

misconceptions.wrong: Putin was elected to succeed Yeltsin in 1999.
misconceptions.right: Yeltsin **resigned** on 31 December 1999 and Putin became acting president; he was elected on 26 March 2000.

Voucher privatisation changed ownership fast; insiders and oligarchs gained most.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent did shock therapy fail to transform the Russian economy between 1992 and 1998?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far shock therapy failed to create a working market economy

modelPlan.thesis: Shock therapy largely failed: it freed prices and changed ownership, but without market institutions it produced hyperinflation, insider privatisation and an economy that lost about 40 per cent of GDP by 1998.

arguments.claim: Freed prices produced hyperinflation and non-payment (named factor first).
Privatisation transferred ownership quickly but to insiders.
The economy lost about 40 per cent of GDP between 1991 and 1998.
The 1998 crash showed the new market was fragile.

modelPlan.counter: Some economists argued there was too little shock, and the 1998 crash cleared the way for growth in 1999–2000.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did a working market economy exist by 1998? No: Hedlund's majority view holds the policy itself at fault, so shock therapy largely failed.

segments.text: Shock therapy largely failed to transform the Russian economy, because it freed prices before the institutions of a market existed.
Hedlund shows that by summer 1992 enterprises met the loss of subsidies with chains of non-payment, and inflation ended the year at well over 2,000 per cent.
This meant that without a bankruptcy law, enterprises could survive without customers, so prices were free but no market discipline followed.
However, privatisation did transfer 70 per cent of enterprises to private hands by June 1994, so ownership was transformed even if markets were not.
Shock therapy therefore changed who owned Russia but largely failed to transform how its economy worked.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Yeltsin did more to undermine democracy in Russia than to build it.” Discuss with reference to the period 1992 to 1999.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim about Yeltsin and democracy
decodeKey.judgement: How far Yeltsin undermined rather than built democracy

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely right: elections continued and Yeltsin left office voluntarily, but force in 1993, oligarchs' money in 1996 and a hand-picked successor in 1999 left a democracy that was, in Sakwa's words, far from consolidated.

arguments.claim: For: October 1993, force and the shutting of the Constitutional Court.
For: the 1996 election bought with oligarchs' money.
Against: a constitution approved by vote and regular elections.
Against: a voluntary resignation under the constitution.

modelPlan.counter: Sakwa argues his claim to be the father of Russian democracy is not without substance, and the democratic path remained open.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Could voters, courts and parliament check power by 1999? Only weakly, so Yeltsin undermined more than he built.

segments.text: Yeltsin did more to undermine democracy than to build it, because he removed the checks on presidential power.
In October 1993 tanks bombarded the parliament, and for three months he shut the Constitutional Court and abolished regional legislatures.
This meant that the constitution approved in December was written by the winner of an armed conflict, so the presidency it created faced few checks.
However, elections continued, the Communists remained the largest party in the Duma, and Yeltsin left office voluntarily in 1999.
The claim is therefore largely valid: Yeltsin kept democracy's forms but weakened its substance.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the constitutional crisis of 1993 in Russia.

decodeKey.verb: Evaluate: weigh strengths and limits, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and how lasting the consequences were

modelPlan.thesis: The crisis was caused mainly by the clash over shock therapy within an unreformed Soviet constitution, and decided by Yeltsin's choice of force; its main consequence was a strong presidency with weak legitimacy.

arguments.claim: Cause: opposition to shock therapy in a parliament with Soviet-era powers.
Cause: Yeltsin's choice of confrontation over compromise.
Consequence: force, near-dictatorial powers and a super-presidential constitution.
Consequence: a weak mandate and a hostile Duma.

modelPlan.counter: The parliament's leaders were no more democratic and also used violence, so blaming Yeltsin alone is unfair.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The strong presidency of the 1993 constitution, which survived the crisis that created it.

segments.text: The crisis of 1993 was caused above all by the clash over shock therapy, but its outcome was decided by Yeltsin's choice of force.
The Congress stripped Yeltsin of his emergency powers in March 1993, and in September his decree 1400 annulled the powers of the legislature.
This meant that the conflict could no longer be settled within the old constitution, so the side with the army won.
However, Rutskoi also urged the crowd to storm the Kremlin and Ostankino, so violence came from both sides.
The crisis therefore produced a strong presidency but, as Reddaway argues, at the cost of Russia's infant democracy.

essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the economic crises of 1992 and 1998 in Russia.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked
decodeKey.judgement: Which differences matter most for judging the 1990s

modelPlan.thesis: Both crises came from a state that could not balance its budget, but they differed in origin and aftermath: 1992 was caused by the reform itself, 1998 by an external shock to a fragile system, and recovery followed only the second.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both rooted in budget deficits the state could not close.
Similarity: both brought a sharp fall in living standards.
Difference: 1992 came from freed prices; 1998 from a global crisis and default.
Difference: 1992 led to years of decline; 1998 was followed by growth.

modelPlan.counter: The two may be one crisis: the 1998 crash was the delayed result of the deficits shock therapy left behind.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference matters most? The aftermath: recovery after 1998 suggests the crash ended a failed model, while 1992 began it.

segments.text: The crises of 1992 and 1998 both came from a state that could not balance its budget, but they differed in origin and outcome.
In 1992 freed prices produced inflation of well over 2,000 per cent, whereas in August 1998 the rouble collapsed and the government defaulted, and GDP fell 5 per cent.
This meant that the first crisis was created by reform itself, while the second exposed a system left fragile by persistent deficits.
However, Hedlund shows the deficits of 1992 haunted the government for years, so the two crises were linked rather than separate.
The decisive difference was therefore the aftermath: decline followed 1992, but growth followed 1998.

segments.text: The war in Chechnya was the most damaging failure of Yeltsin's first term.
Launched on 11 December 1994 by hardliners who expected a quick victory, it lasted until August 1996 and killed between 2 and 10 per cent of Chechnya's population.
This meant that Yeltsin entered the 1996 campaign with an unpopular war, so it became one of the four problems that pushed his ratings into single digits.
However, he still won in 1996, helped by a new peace plan and the oligarchs' money, so the war weakened but did not destroy his presidency.
The war's impact was therefore severe on his standing but not decisive for his survival.

essayQuestions.text: Analyse the reasons why Yeltsin won the presidential election of 1996.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its reasons and show how they connect

modelPlan.thesis: Yeltsin won mainly because the oligarchs financed a campaign that outspent his rivals; tactical moves on Chechnya and his ministers, and the choice against a Communist return, completed it.

arguments.claim: The oligarchs bankrolled the campaign; the spending cap was broken.
A skilled campaign team: Chubais and Dyachenko.
Tactical moves: sacking liberal ministers and a Chechnya peace plan.
A run-off against the Communist Zyuganov.

modelPlan.counter: His heart attack was hidden from voters, so his victory also rested on what the voters did not know.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without which reason would he have lost? The oligarchs' money, because his ratings were in single digits before the campaign.

segments.text: Yeltsin won the 1996 election mainly because the oligarchs financed a campaign he could not otherwise have fought.
With approval ratings in single digits, he relied on a campaign run by Chubais and Dyachenko and bankrolled by the oligarchs, and the Kremlin admitted exceeding the spending cap.
This meant that a deeply unpopular president could outspend his rivals and reach a run-off against the Communist Zyuganov.
However, his heart attack between the rounds was hidden from voters, so he won partly because of what the electorate did not know.
The oligarchs' money was therefore the decisive reason, and, as Sakwa argues, its price was oligarchic capitalism.
